lesson.title: Never Assume, Always Default
lesson.summary: A default value is a planned fallback used when something is missing, and dictionaries support this pattern directly through get() and setdefault().
lesson.body:
You have already met default values in the context of functions: a parameter like def greet(name, greeting="Hello") supplies a fallback value that is used automatically whenever the caller does not provide one. Dictionaries lean on this exact same idea. The get() method you learned earlier is really a default value mechanism: dictionary.get(key, default) says 'use this value if the key was never provided.'

def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Sam"))

inventory = {"pens": 12}
print(inventory.get("pencils", 0))

This prints Hello, Sam!, then 0. The function call reuses the default greeting because none was supplied, and the dictionary lookup reuses the default 0 because "pencils" was never stocked. Both are the same underlying idea, a planned answer for the case where something expected is absent, just applied to two different parts of the language.

This pattern becomes especially powerful for counting. Whenever you need a running tally keyed by something, get(key, 0) lets you treat an unseen key as if it already held a zero.

count = {}
for letter in "banana":
    count[letter] = count.get(letter, 0) + 1
print(count)

This prints {'b': 1, 'a': 3, 'n': 2}. On the very first "b", count.get("b", 0) returns 0 because "b" is not in count yet, and adding 1 gives 1. By the time the loop reaches the last "a", count.get("a", 0) returns the 2 that has already accumulated, and adding 1 brings it to 3. Without the default of 0, this line would raise a KeyError the very first time a new letter appeared.

Python's dictionaries also offer a close cousin of get() called setdefault(). Calling inventory.setdefault("pencils", 0) behaves like get() when the key is missing, except it also inserts the key with that default value into the dictionary at the same time, so the next lookup finds it already there. get() only reads, setdefault() reads and writes, and choosing between them comes down to whether you want the missing key to actually become part of the dictionary going forward.
